newsitem.title: GERMANY: "Independence Day" breaks German box office record.
newsitem.headline: "Independence Day" breaks German box office record.

text.p: "Independence Day", a German-directed Hollywood action film about invading space aliens, smashed opening weekend box office records in Germany, film industry officials said on Tuesday.

Directed by German-born expatriate Roland Emmerich, "Independence Day" earned 22,628,312 marks ($14.96 million) and attracted 1,918,566 people in its first four days to knock the 1993 hit "Jurassic Park" into second place.
The film has set records in many countries since its U.S. debut in July and pulled in more than $290 million in the U.S. alone.
But the film's producers, 20th Century Fox, had especially high hopes for Germany, the world's second largest film market after the United States, because of Emmerich's German roots.

"There was an enormous amount of media hype in advance about the film and especially Emmerich so it seemed a good bet that 'Independence Day' would break a lot of records," said Monica Herrin of the association of German film distributors.

She said "Independence Day's" start had beaten "Jurassic Park" by nearly four million marks and it seemed likely to surpass the 90-million-mark cumulative German gross for the 1993 Steven Spielberg film.
"Independence Day" is a science-fiction action film about an invasion of aliens who launch a coordinated attack from enormous space ships and destroy cities around the globe.
But the aliens are ultimately defeated after the world's nations join together with patriotic Americans.
Theatres sold out nationwide during the first four days.
One film centre in Frankfurt had the film running on 10 of its 12 screens for the opening night, and Berlin's 1,052-seat Zoo Palace was sold out for near round the clock screenings.

"I've never seen anything like this," said Jenny Vogt, the manager at Zoo Palace after all five Monday night performances were sold out. More than 600 people came for one Sunday morning screening that began at 2.15 a.m. and ran until 5 a.m.
"It is a shame that we have had to turn so many people away," she added. "It seems everyone in Germany feels that they have to see this film."
"Independence Day" set another record by making its debut on 855 of Germany's 3,900 screens, so more than one in five theatres are now showing it.
The film was boosted by heavy German media attention on Emmerich, a 40-year-old director who left Germany seven years ago after regularly being bashed by high-brow German film critics.

Emmerich has been toasted as a returning hero during the last week, giving long interviews to every important newspaper and television programme. Asked by Der Spiegel magazine if he wanted to make films in Germany again, Emmerich replied:
"No, because in Germany there is neither the right attitude nor the money for the type of films I make...

"People are always whining here about this or that. People are always doubting themselves. The thing I miss most about Germany is the good Havana cigars I can get here. They are very hard to come by in Hollywood." ($1=1.5124 Mark)
